tasks.locator: Materials and Method › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 514-515)
tasks.extracted: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person study of 16 volunteers (12 men and 4 women, aged 21 to 39) in four counterbalanced conditions at least 14 days apart: placebo then placebo, citalopram then placebo, placebo then MDMA, citalopram then MDMA. Citalopram 40 mg (or saline) was infused over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) was taken by mouth, and ratings were made 120 minutes after MDMA. Six volunteers had tried recreational drugs before: two ecstasy, three a hallucinogen and one both. Editors' count: 3 of the 16 had tried ecstasy and 13 had not.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (pp. 515-516); Figure 1 (p. 516); Table 1 (p. 517)
tasks.extracted: MDMA raised all three altered-state scales against placebo (Rao R(3,12)=7.25, P<.005) and citalopram pretreatment lowered them (pretreatment by treatment: oceanic boundlessness F(1,15)=22.47, anxious ego dissolution F(1,15)=23.04, visionary restructuralization F(1,15)=12.80). Item clusters, percent of maximum, MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA: positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1; of the 15 item clusters, MDMA significantly raised 13, and citalopram significantly lowered 10 of those 13 but not frightening derealization, synesthesia or facilitated recollection. Editors' calculation from the printed means: the ten lowered clusters fell by about 55 to 80 percent.

tasks.locator: Results, last paragraph (p. 516); Figure 2 (p. 518); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 517) and the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (pp. 518-519)
tasks.extracted: On the mood scales, citalopram lowered the MDMA-induced rises in self-confidence (P<.04) and extroversion (P<.01) to the level of citalopram alone, and efficiency-activation (P<.03); the fall in heightened mood did not reach significance (P=.06), and the rises in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not lowered at all. Citalopram alone lowered some scale scores against placebo, which the authors put down mostly to its side effects (fatigue, headache and nausea; nausea in 6 of 16).

tasks.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Another interesting finding' and the continuation of the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (p. 519)
tasks.extracted: MDMA's subjective effect lasted a mean of 3 hours; after citalopram it was markedly reduced but lasted a mean of 5 hours, stated without a method, spread or test. No blood concentrations were taken. The authors put the lowering at about 60 percent and note that all received the same 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kilogram and the size of the lowering; in a pilot, two people given 60 or 80 mg of citalopram had MDMA's effects blocked to a degree comparable with 40 mg.

tasks.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 955)
tasks.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 24; all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; MDMA taken on at least 5 earlier occasions). Two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, with MDMA 100 mg on day 3, 3 hours after that day's capsule. A 13th man withdrew after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety) and never took MDMA.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 957); Results › Physiological Effects and Subjective Effects (p. 957); Figs. 1 to 3 (pp. 958-960)
tasks.extracted: Paroxetine lowered MDMA's effects: peak systolic pressure 12 mm Hg lower (Emax F=22.20, P=0.001), diastolic 5 mm Hg and heart rate 14 beats/min lower, pupil widening from 3.33 to 1.23 mm (F=70.35, P<0.001), temperature rise 0.3 C lower (P=0.041); ARCI euphoria scale (morphine-benzedrine group) peak 7.27 to 4; VESSPA anxiety 5.55 to 2.7, sociability 3.0 to 0.58, activity 5.91 to 1.21; visual-analogue 'stimulated', 'high', 'any effect', 'good effects' and 'liking' lower (all P=0.003 or less at peak). By Table 1 the diastolic area (P=0.613) and peak (P=0.213) and the heart-rate area (P=0.093) were not significant.

tasks.locator: Results › Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957-958); Table 2 (p. 961)
tasks.extracted: MDMA with paroxetine against placebo (n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L, both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and area 1189.47 against 1923.32, half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01); MDMA half-life 8.34 against 7.88 hours. The paper's own text gives MDMA 22 (exposure) and 16% (peak) higher and HMMA 39 (exposure) and 49% (peak) lower. Editors' calculation from the printed means: HMMA exposure -38%.

tasks.locator: Abstract (p. 954); Table 1 and Results › Subjective Effects (p. 957); Discussion, final paragraph (pp. 961-962)
tasks.extracted: Ratings of bad effects, fear, and depression or sadness did not change significantly with paroxetine, and no hallucinations, psychotic symptoms or serious adverse events were seen. The authors write that the marked decrease in positive effects may lead to higher MDMA doses (they give people with depression who take SSRIs as an example) and so to potentially life-threatening toxicity; no extra MDMA was given in the study, so this is their inference. The abstract gives the rise in MDMA level as 30%, a figure taken in the Discussion from an earlier 7-man analysis; the trial's own figures are 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure to 21 hours).
tasks.quote: could lead users to take higher doses of MDMA

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 529)
tasks.extracted: The authors write that a single recreational dose of MDMA inhibits CYP2D6 rapidly and completely whereas several prescription doses of paroxetine are needed, that citalopram and paroxetine block the positive effects of MDMA, and that people taking an SSRI together with multiple doses of MDMA should know that the metabolism of both substances is compromised, with a possible increase in the risk of acute adverse effects already reported for poor metabolizers. The reference given for people taking SSRIs to change MDMA's effects is a rat study. No SSRI was given with MDMA in this study.

tasks.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 526); Drugs, 1st paragraph; Study Design, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 526-527)
tasks.extracted: Fifteen healthy men (mean age 26, range 19 to 33; on average 26 previous MDMA experiences) who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening, recruited by word of mouth and paid. Open, fixed-order design: session 1 (control, dextromethorphan 30 mg with caffeine 100 mg), then at least 3 days later session 2 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 75 to 100 mg, with caffeine and dextromethorphan 30 mg at 4 hours and later); the dextromethorphan schedule was 4, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 168 hours in the first 3 men and 4, 24, 72, 96, 168 and 240 hours in the other 12, because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours; results pooled. No placebo MDMA session.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 528)
tasks.extracted: Plasma probe drug after MDMA against the control session (Table 1, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL (SDs 3.6 and 18.5) and area over 8 hours 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9 and area 1877.1 to 179.1; 3-hydroxymorphinan peak 164.1 to 16.6 and area 764.2 to 97.5 (all P<0.05); 3-methoxymorphinan not significantly changed. The authors say the dextromethorphan peak and area increased approximately 10-fold. MDMA peak 194.3 ng/mL (SD 30.9) at 2.0 hours (SD 1.0). Editors' calculation from the printed means: 8.5-fold for the peak and 9.5-fold for the area.

tasks.locator: Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2
tasks.extracted: The urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio rose from 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), which the authors call almost 100-fold; 67% of the men had a value above 0.3, the cut-off for assigning the poor-metabolizer phenotype, after MDMA; no correlation of the ratio with urine pH (r=0.049) or creatinine (r=0.214). Recovery fitted one exponential curve: rate constant 0.016 (SD 0.005) per hour, recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8), r2=0.791. Editors' calculation: the ratio of the printed means is 71-fold, and 67% of 15 men is 10 men.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (pp. 528-529); 3rd paragraph (p. 529)
tasks.extracted: The ratio had not recovered fully to its basal level at 10 days; the half-life corrected for MDMA's own residence time is 37.4 hours (SD 11.6), and the authors think it underestimates recovery because activity had not recovered even at 10 days; a two-phase fit gives 103.0 hours (SD 70.3), corrected 93.7 (SD 70.4), though variability and few time points question the biphasic model. Editors' reading: the first probe dose after MDMA was given 4 hours after it, when MDMA was near its peak, so competition for the enzyme cannot be separated from its inactivation in the early hours.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 528); Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 528)
tasks.extracted: In 15 men, a single MDMA dose of 1.5 mg/kg raised the exposure to the CYP2D6 probe drug dextromethorphan from 15.7 to 149.1 (area over 8 hours) and its peak from 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL, lowered the product dextrorphan from 464.6 to 31.9 ng/mL at peak, and raised the urinary probe-drug to product ratio from 0.0061 to 0.4322; the recovery half-life was 46.6 hours (SD 11.8) on one fit, and the ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 529)
tasks.extracted: The authors recall their own earlier study in which MDMA concentrations were increased beyond what accumulation predicts when a second dose was taken 24 hours later. They also write that people who use MDMA are known to take on average more than 1 pill per session (1.8 to 2.9 pills on average, up to 6 to 7 depending on the type of person, citing their reference 36, which was not read) and that many binge for several days, and infer, without having given a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher plasma concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. No second dose, concentration-effect measure or toxicity outcome was studied here (editors' reading).

tasks.locator: Research letter, 3rd paragraph (the summary above the text counted as the 1st; begins 'The UK National Teratology Information Service')
tasks.extracted: The UK National Teratology Information Service followed up 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with ecstasy exposure from January 1989 to June 1998; there were 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.

tasks.locator: Research letter, 5th and 6th paragraphs (begin '74 pregnant women reported' and '127 women')
tasks.extracted: 74 women reported ecstasy only and 62 ecstasy with other drugs of abuse (amphetamine 37, cocaine 20, cannabis 16, alcohol 13, LSD nine, other 13); acute toxicity from ecstasy in two mothers. 127 women (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs) were exposed in the first trimester, two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy.

tasks.locator: Research letter, 7th and 8th paragraphs (begin '11 pregnancies resulted in miscarriage' and 'There were 78 liveborn infants'); summary above the text; Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)
tasks.extracted: 11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage (8%, within the expected range) and 48 in elective termination (35%, higher than the UK average; one after prenatal diagnosis of malformations); no necropsy data on the other aborted fetuses; by subtraction (editors' arithmetic) the other 77 pregnancies gave the 78 live-born infants, one pair being twins. 78 live-born infants: 66 normal and 12 with congenital anomalies, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), described as significantly higher than an expected incidence of 2 to 3%, with no test or P value given; the summary calls this a possible association with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects; the table lists 13 anomaly findings (12 live-born, plus one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs), among them a toe under its neighbour, plagiocephaly, pyloric stenosis, ptosis, pigmentation of a thigh and clicking hips. No source is given for the expected incidence.
tasks.quote: may be associated with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects

tasks.locator: Research letter, 9th and 10th paragraphs (begin 'Eight infants were born prematurely' and 'No adverse effects were observed in the sex ratio')
tasks.extracted: Eight infants were born prematurely (25 to 36 weeks, including twins at 25 weeks; two fetal distress cases thought unrelated to ecstasy); one neonatal death in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy; no adverse effect on sex ratio; birthweights within the expected range for term infants, with only three under 2.5 kg.

tasks.locator: Research letter, 11th and 12th paragraphs (begin 'There were three female infants with talipes' and 'The spontaneous incidence of congenital heart disease'); summary above the text
tasks.extracted: Three female infants had talipes (38 per 1000, CI 8 to 109, against an expected 1 per 1000; the letter says idiopathic talipes is male-predominant 3 to 1 in the UK); two infants had congenital heart disease, ventricular septal defects (26 per 1000, CI 3.0 to 90.0, against an expected 5 to 10 per 1000). The authors say the small series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly but consider the data important. Editors' reading of the table: the three infants with talipes were in the ecstasy-only group, and both infants with a ventricular septal defect had other drug exposure.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the 1970s to the early 1990s', 1st paragraph (p. 235); Table 1, Renfroe row (p. 236)
tasks.extracted: Renfroe (1986), as summarized: of 610 samples of MDA or MDMA among 20,721 street drug samples sent to a Californian laboratory between 1972 and 1985, 12% (89 samples) were submitted under the names MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy. The large majority of those 89 held MDMA or MDMA with MDA; only two held neither (a capsule from Honolulu with an amphetamine compound, and a largely empty plastic syringe from Miami labelled ecstasy/speed). Table 1 gives 97% (n=87) containing MDMA or MDA.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s', 1st paragraph (begins p. 235, ends p. 236); Table 2, Spruit (2001) 1993–1997 row (p. 236)
tasks.extracted: Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System, as summarized from Spruit (2001): set up in 1992; samples were not collected systematically, most being brought in by individual people who wanted to know what a pill held; each pill was quick-tested and those not identified were sent for laboratory analysis (on average more than 100 pills a week). In each year from 1993 to 1996 about 48–60% of pills held MDMA alone, 12–20% MDEA alone, 2–5% MDA alone, 7–13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or other drugs, 1–4% amphetamine alone and 2–7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA; over 80% held an amphetamine-type drug; 6–17% held other drugs outside that class (hallucinogens such as LSD and ketamine, atropine, caffeine, paracetamol or unknown compounds). In 1997 44% held MDMA alone, 14% MDMA plus another drug, 24% MDA, MDEA or amphetamine and 18% other non-amphetamine drugs; the review links the dip to difficulty in obtaining the chemical precursor. The share holding MDMA rose to 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999. Table 2 gives, for 1993–1997, 44–60% MDMA only, 9–25% MDEA or MDA only, 16–25% mixtures and 6–18% others.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 1st paragraph; Table 3, Schifano (2000), Spruit (2001) and Palenicek et al. (2002) rows (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: Italy, as quoted from Schifano (2000): forensic laboratories had examined at least 20,000 tablets in five years; about 85–90% of tablets seized in the north-east held MDMA as the active ingredient, in amounts of 100–150 mg a tablet; MDA and MDEA were usually in the remainder, phenylbutanamine occasionally, and dummy tablets about 1% of the material (Table 3: 85–90% MDMA, 8–10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others). Netherlands 1999: around 81% held MDMA (Table 3: 81% MDMA only, 19% all others). Czech Republic, Palenicek et al. (2002): 120 pills and capsules analysed between 1998 and 2002 (Table 3 says 1998–2001), over 80% held only MDMA; the rest held amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDEA, ketamine, ephedrine, MDA or mixtures (Table 3: more than 80% MDMA, 4% MDA, under 16% others and mixtures).

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Hansen et al. (2001) noted'; it continues on p. 238); Table 3, Winstock et al. row (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: Hansen et al. (2001), as summarized: people in Australia who used ecstasy and were surveyed between 1998 and 2000 estimated that about one tablet in every four or five was a dud; the review says this ratio is close to the more systematic survey data from Italy, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic. Winstock et al. (2001) surveyed 1151 dance clubbers in June 1999 about beliefs, consumption and perceptions of quality; Table 3 gives subjective reports of recent improvements in the quality of supplies.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph, the part on p. 238 beginning 'The American website www.dancesafe.org' (the paragraph begins on p. 237); Table 3, Cole et al., Dancesafe and Ramsey (2003) rows (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: A US website, Dancesafe.org, listed tablets sent in for commercial analysis: about 175 tablets in 2002, of which 88% held MDMA alone or in combination and 4% held MDE or MDA (alone or in a combination without MDMA); Table 3 adds 4% others and 4% no identifiable drug. Ramsey et al. (2001): in samples from an amnesty bin at the entrance of a London dance venue, a high proportion of the tablets held MDMA and the powders were mostly amphetamine. Ramsey (2003), asked for later findings: the tablets in the bins were almost all MDMA. Cole et al. (2002): 136 tablets submitted to the Forensic Science Service in north-west England in 2001 all held MDMA by liquid chromatography.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has been described')
tasks.extracted: The review's own estimates of the share of ecstasy tablets holding MDMA: from the 1980s to the early 1990s around 90–98%, the remaining 2–10% generally MDA; in the mid to late 1990s between 50 and 80%, with around 5–30% holding MDA or MDEA and around 4–20% other drugs; in the late 1990s around 80–95% (citing Spruit and Winstock et al.); in the early 2000s values approaching 100% in the most recent surveys (citing Cole et al. and Ramsey).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'These estimates can, however, only be seen as very approximate')
tasks.extracted: The review calls its estimates very approximate because the empirical evidence is limited: only three reports covered large samples over a long period (a US anonymous testing service, Renfroe 1986; the Dutch monitoring project, Spruit 2001; northern Italy, Schifano 2000), and the smaller surveys largely confirmed them. It adds that no study used a randomized sampling procedure; most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins; police seizures of large batches of uniform tablets may overestimate purity (Cole et al. 2002); and a US service charged $100 for each pill analysed (Baggott et al. 2000), far more than its street value, which probably led to a preponderance of atypical drugs.
tasks.quote: no study has employed a randomized sampling procedure

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has practical consequences')
tasks.extracted: The review says that when a tablet holds MDA or MDEA, whose effects on brain chemistry are similar to those of MDMA, people would probably not notice any marked difference except possibly in how long the effect lasts or in subtle details of the experience (citing Hegadoren et al. 1999). In the Dutch data, even in the years with the lowest share of MDMA (1994 and 1997) the large majority of tablets still held MDMA, MDEA or MDA, and at other periods the match between ecstasy and MDMA was often around 90%.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'However, a substantial minority of ecstasy tablets')
tasks.extracted: The review states that a substantial minority of tablets held other compounds: between 1993 and 1997, 6–18% of Dutch samples held other drugs outside the amphetamine class. It says the effects of ketamine are so different from MDMA that taking it unknowingly could be extremely distressing, and reports that 4-methylthioamphetamine (4-MTA) was found in amnesty bins and, in the words of the authors it cites, had been implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands. A small proportion of tablets held weak substances (paracetamol, caffeine, placebo) and others held atropine, opiates, phenylbutanamine or dextromethorphan; the review says the acute effects of these could be unexpected and unpleasant.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'One intriguing question is why the supplies of ecstasy first became problematical')
tasks.extracted: The review says people who use ecstasy were fully aware of the quality problems of the mid-1990s and, when interviewed, can readily tell the occasions when they feel they have taken MDMA from their other experiences; jaw clenching, tooth grinding and the quality of mood changes are used to gauge the purity and strength of tablets, and one qualitative study described early nausea as a subjective sign. It adds that uncertainty over purity led many potential people to avoid illicit drugs, while regular ones often became more wary and took supplies only from friends. These are people's impressions; the review does not compare them with analyses of the tablets.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic', pp. 239–240)
tasks.extracted: Amounts of MDMA per tablet, as summarized: most Italian samples held 100–150 mg in 1995–2000 (Schifano 2000); UK annual averages were 90–102 mg between 1991 and 1995 and 73–88 mg between 1996 and 2001 (Cole et al. 2002). Small UK studies in the mid-1990s found amounts that were variable and often low: some tablets held 100–140 mg, others about 50 mg and some under 20 mg (Sherlock et al. 1999). In the Czech Republic tablets varied from 30 to 100 mg, with 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose) at the extremes (Palenicek et al. 2002). 80 white tablets from a large UK police seizure in 2001 held 73–89 mg, mean 79 mg (Cole et al. 2002). The Dutch monitoring met high-amount tablets occasionally in 1998. The review calls unknown amount a key area of uncertainty, says that high-amount tablets may be particularly dangerous for people taking MDMA for the first time because they could cause a severe serotonin syndrome reaction (no data given), and notes that two sources found no analytic evidence of toxic contaminants in MDMA batches (King 2000; Schifano 2000).

tasks.locator: 2.1 Complicating issues in generalising laboratory research to recreational human use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The review notes that pills sold as ecstasy may not contain MDMA at all, so people developing regular or dependent use of ecstasy may not be taking MDMA, and that some or many pills may contain methamphetamine, so people may develop dependence on methamphetamine rather than, or as well as, MDMA. Some studies controlled statistically for other drug use, including methamphetamine, but that use was self-reported, not confirmed by laboratory testing.

tasks.locator: Table 1, rows Stone et al. to Bruno et al. (p. 4)
tasks.extracted: Population-based samples: Stone et al. (US National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse, 2000-2001; N 1199; six items matching DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria): 3.8% past year, among people who had started ecstasy within the previous two years. Von Sydow et al. (Germany, 1995-1999; representative sample aged 14-24; N 207; CIDI interview): 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy; less than 10% of those classed as lifetime dependent were past-year dependent at the 42-month follow-up. Wu et al. (US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 2005; N 652; the same six hallucinogen items): 3.6% past year; another 11% reported one or two symptoms. Samples of sentinel populations: Parsons et al. (New York nightclub attendees aged 18-29 who had used ecstasy in the past 4 weeks; N 214; CIDI): 19% past year, with a median of 2.5 days of use in the past 4 months. Yen and Hsu (Taiwanese juvenile justice detainees who had used ecstasy; N 200): 22% past year. Self-selected sample: Bruno et al. (Australia, 2003-2004; N 1662; people using ecstasy at least monthly, recruited by purposive and snowball sampling; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 4 or more): 18% past month; among those screening positively, 49% used 1-2 times per week and 34% 1-2 times per month.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (continued), rows Cottler et al. to Thomasius et al. (p. 5)
tasks.extracted: Cottler et al. (US; adolescents and young adults in inpatient drug treatment and in the community, at least 5 lifetime occasions of use; N 52; computerised CIDI module): 43% lifetime; the most common symptoms were continued use despite problems (63%) and withdrawal (59%), and all dependent participants had tolerance or withdrawal. Hanson and Luciana (US students and community members; N 26; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): the prevalence cell reads N = 2 LT while the details column says 14 met the criteria. Scheier et al. (US and Australia; N 639; modified CIDI): no prevalence given, mean 227 lifetime pills. Topp et al. (Australia, 1997; N 185; CIDI): 64% lifetime; the authors questioned how withdrawal symptoms were endorsed. Tossman (Germany, 2002; N 195; people who used ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year): 16%, timeframe not specified. Yacoubian et al. (Washington rave attendees; N 154; a screening scale): 17% lifetime, 'probable' dependence. Thomasius et al. (Germany; rave attendees with at least 250 lifetime tablets, mean 794; N 59; clinical interview rated by clinical psychologists): 73% lifetime.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (continued), Winstock et al. row, and footnote; 3.2 Studies of ecstasy dependence among users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6)
tasks.extracted: Winstock et al. (UK, 1999; readers of a dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy; N 1106; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 5 or more): 17%, with a footnote that the timeframe was not specified; mean 160 lifetime occasions of use; tolerance and continued use despite problems with health, work or relationships were reported by more than half of the sample. Section 3.2: few studies have examined dependence among people who use ecstasy; all used instruments designed for other drugs, and just one (of a non-representative sample) involved clinician or psychiatric assessment. Topp et al. (1997): 64% of 185 people who regularly used ecstasy met lifetime criteria, typically during their heaviest use period, when 66% were using 1-2 times per week and 25% between 1 and 3 days per month; the authors questioned whether the withdrawal items separated comedown effects from dysphoria that eases with further use.

tasks.locator: 3.2, the paragraph beginning 'Two large survey samples of dependence' and the paragraph beginning 'Studies of dependence among ecstasy users in representative general population samples are limited'
tasks.extracted: Two large samples used the five-item Severity of Dependence Scale, which measures compulsion to use: in the UK survey of 1106 dance-magazine readers 17% screened positive for lifetime ecstasy dependence, and in the Australian interview-based study of 1662 people who regularly used ecstasy, 18% screened positive; of these 49% used ecstasy 1-2 times per week, 34% used 1-3 times per month and only 2% (n = 7) were using at least every second day, and financial, legal and work harms, sexual risk, overdose and help seeking were more common than among those who screened negative, independent of problematic methamphetamine use. In general population samples a German study found that past-year ecstasy/hallucinogen/stimulant dependence among all young adults was 0.4%; a US study found that 4% of people who had used ecstasy in the past year met DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria (another 11% reported one or two symptoms) (Wu et al.), and 3.82% of those who had started ecstasy in the previous two years had developed dependence (Stone et al.); some have argued that grouping ecstasy with the hallucinogens in DSM-IV may not fit the behavioural data.

tasks.locator: 3.3 The structure of ecstasy dependence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd begins on p. 7 and ends on p. 8)
tasks.extracted: Two studies of the structure of the symptoms, both in Australian samples (one also in US samples): Topp et al. (1997) found for ecstasy, unlike alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids, two separate components, compulsive use (use despite problems, giving up activities, unsuccessful attempts to stop, withdrawal, excessive time spent) and escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended); Bruno et al. (2009) found two related factors with the same names for the Severity of Dependence Scale. tasks.extracted: Limitations: the studies are extremely heterogeneous in assessment methods and samples, which makes meta-analysis inappropriate; dependence was typically assessed by self-report without clinician verification, usually as lifetime retrospective reports; despite relatively infrequent use even at their heaviest, people very commonly reported dependence symptoms, and it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as the investigators intended; the prevalence cannot be extrapolated to all people who use ecstasy because most studies recruited people with recent use by convenience or snowball sampling; information on the natural history comes mostly from retrospective reports of convenience samples. Summary: the review judges the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome to be restricted in how much was studied and in how it was studied (see the quotation); animal evidence suggests MDMA may be a less potent reinforcer than other drugs but still has dependence potential; some people report problems controlling their use and concern about it, but there is a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal, which suggests physical symptoms play a more limited role than psychological ones; tolerance and withdrawal have been reported, mostly in questionnaires designed for other drugs; treatment presentations are uncommon compared with the prevalence of use but do occur.

Limitations the authors state: postmortem redistribution may alter drug concentrations (some specimens were taken days after death, for example six days in case 18, or from non-peripheral sites such as cavity blood in case 10); missing information, including the source of the drugs (prescribing information) and clinical data such as temperature; people are usually found dead, so symptoms go unreported; and concentrations of drugs that produce tolerance, such as morphine, are hard to interpret. tasks.extracted: The Hunter Area Toxicology Service is a regional toxicology unit; every overdose presentation and admission is entered prospectively into a clinical database by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses. Of 9960 admissions between 13 January 1987 and 22 November 2002, 2222 involved at least one serotonergic drug taken in overdose; this test dataset had no exclusions and includes the derivation dataset. Of the 473, 73 (15.4%, 95%CI 12.3–19.0) had a diagnosis of serotonin toxicity made by a clinical toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 95%CI 11.7–18.4) met Sternbach's criteria and 44 (9.3%, 95%CI 6.8–12.3) were treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist. The tree analysis was done in the SSRI-alone dataset; the rules were tested on the complete dataset. The paper reports no ages, sex, drugs or amounts.

tasks.locator: Results › Life-threatening serotonin toxicity (single paragraph)
tasks.extracted: Life-threatening cases were those intubated and ventilated. Forty-two patients were intubated for a decreased Glasgow Coma Score or for decontamination; six were intubated solely for worsening serotonin toxicity. All six had a high fever and multiple features of serotonin toxicity. Progressive rigidity compromising respiratory function was the precipitating event; the preceding signs were a high fever (above 38.5 C) and increasing, particularly truncal, rigidity and peripheral hypertonicity. tasks.extracted: The authors write that serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum of toxicity rather than a defined clinical entity with clear prognostic importance, and so call it serotonin toxicity; that it results from an increase in serotonin in the synapses of the central nervous system, so is a concentration-dependent toxicity that can develop in any individual and not an idiosyncratic reaction; and that it can be thought of as a triad of autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status.

tasks.locator: Opening paragraph; Definition and epidemiology, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review calls the serotonin syndrome a potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction, a predictable consequence of excess serotonin stimulation of receptors, with clinical manifestations from barely perceptible to lethal. It is often described as a triad of mental-status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular abnormalities, but not all are present in every person; signs range from tremor and diarrhoea in mild cases to delirium, neuromuscular rigidity and hyperthermia in life-threatening cases; mild symptoms may be easily overlooked.

tasks.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning To better delineate the signs and symptoms (p. 1114); Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 1115)
tasks.extracted: The review describes its source as the clinical findings in 2222 consecutive cases of self-poisoning with serotonergic drugs from a toxicology registry, compared with the gold standard of a medical toxicologist's diagnosis, and says its preferred decision rules are simpler, more sensitive (84 percent against 75 percent) and more specific (97 percent against 96 percent) than the original criteria. It does not say that the figures come from one unit or that the rules were derived in part of the same records, gives no intervals, and does not mention the source paper's statement that no gold standard exists.

tasks.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, 1st paragraph; How does it present?, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review describes serotonin syndrome, also called serotonin toxicity, as a drug-induced cluster of dose-related adverse effects due to increased serotonin in the central nervous system, covering a spectrum from mild to severe. It says toxicity starts within hours of ingesting the drugs and that the classic triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (hyperthermia, tachycardia) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion).

tasks.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning Some pathognomonic features)
tasks.extracted: The review calls generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) the classic feature and the key component of the Hunter criteria, which it says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited for this statement is the derivation paper (reference 13). It describes spontaneous clonus as rhythmic, large muscle contractions, often triggered by minor movements or vibrations and easily brought out with ankle dorsiflexion, and ocular clonus as fine or coarse oscillations of gaze in all directions.

tasks.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state

It describes the typical picture as agitation or hypervigilance with tremor and exaggerated reflexes, with muscle spasms starting in the lower limbs and becoming generalised, then fever, sweating, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate and rapid breathing, and fixed rigidity in severe cases.

He describes a 1968 experiment (Evans-Prosser) in which 15 patients were given injections of pethidine, morphine or water in graduated doses in hospital, in blind random order (study condition: top single pethidine dose 75 mg, morphine 7.5 mg); none had serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus were not examined, only pulse and arterial pressure. He reads this as confirming that weak reuptake inhibitors like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity, but only in susceptible individuals or with particularly large doses. He says the complete list of references on serotonin toxicity and analgesics, located through a search of the listed papers and standard databases (approximately 40), is on his website; that pethidine has undoubtedly caused a number of severe reactions and some fatalities, and the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics also some fatalities; that a small series using usual therapeutic doses may lead to a false sense of security because the dose–effect relationship is not sufficiently appreciated; and that differences in cytochrome P450 enzymes produce 20–50-fold variations in serum levels between patients.

tasks.extracted: The reviewer says the limited clinical and experimental data agree that morphine analogues (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine) are not reuptake inhibitors, none precipitates serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and there are no reports with them; that the phenylpiperidine opioids (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl and congeners, dextromethorphan, propoxyphene) are probably all borderline, weak reuptake inhibitors, implicated in multiple reports that are almost certainly serotonin toxicity as judged by a subjective interpretation of the old case reports; that about 40 cases involving analgesics are in his updated review; and that all the opioid analgesics with serotonergic effects have been involved in serotonin toxicity reports but none of the drugs without reuptake-inhibiting capacity have. For fentanyl he judges one case report with a fatality (cardiac surgery in a patient on MAOIs) probably a result of serotonin toxicity and another possibly an unrecognised case, says there is a question mark over fentanyl, that it has probably been used in many unreported cases with MAOIs without a problem, and that there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate of the risk.

tasks.locator: Conclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The conclusion says morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and that pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and methadone definitely are weak reuptake inhibitors and may infrequently precipitate dose-dependent serotonin toxicity with any type of MAOI, but perhaps only in large doses or susceptible individuals. The ability to estimate the risk is said to be compromised by a lack of systematically recorded clinical data and of precise potency data; for propoxyphene, pentazocine, fentanyl, remifentanil and congeners there are no reuptake affinity data, so interpolation and the presence or absence of clinical reports are used. The reviewer writes that the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low, but its unpredictable and serious nature makes it difficult to form judgments, and that any reaction is dose-dependent.
